# Chronic suppurative otitis media

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Head and neck surgery > Chronic suppurative otitis media*

[Original Article Link](/library/bF0Hg3)

---

## Summary

Chronic suppurative <u>otitis media</u> (CSOM) is characterized by at least 2 weeks–3 months of inflammation and infection of the <u>middle ear</u> in patients with a <u>nonintact tympanic membrane</u> (TM). CSOM is one of the most common <u>causes of hearing loss</u> in low-income countries where it typically affects children under 5 years of age. Infections in CSOM are usually polymicrobial. <u>Risk factors</u> include <u>recurrent acute otitis media</u>, frequent <u>upper respiratory tract infections</u>, and poor <u>nutritional status</u>. Patients typically report painless, recurrent discharge from <u>the ear</u> and <u>hearing loss</u>. CSOM is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> supported by a thorough history and otoscopic findings of <u>otorrhea</u> and a <u>perforated TM</u>. <u>Hearing loss</u> should be evaluated with diagnostic <u>hearing</u> tests. For uncomplicated infections, <u>conservative treatment</u> with topical medications (i.e., <u>antibiotics</u> +/- <u>steroids</u>) is preferred. <u>Neuroimaging</u>, <u>laboratory studies</u>, systemic antimicrobials, and/or <u>surgery</u> may be indicated for patients with persistent CSOM that does not respond to <u>conservative measures</u>. If left untreated, the infection may spread and result in extracranial and intracranial <u>CNS</u> complications. <u>Primary prevention</u> and timely <u>management of acute otitis media</u> are essential to preventing CSOM.




See also “<u>Acute otitis media</u>” and “<u>Otitis media with effusion</u>.”

---

## Epidemiology

* North America: < 1% <u>prevalence</u> across all ages (adults and children) [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)

* Globally

* 4–10% <u>prevalence</u> in some regions

* Most common in children ≤ 5 years of age (peak at ∼ 2 years) [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)





> [!TIP]
> In many low-income countries, CSOM is the most common cause of <u>hearing loss</u>. [[3]](/library/scWtd40)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### Common pathogens [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[3]](/library/scWtd40)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)




CSOM is typically a polymicrobial infection that may include any of the following pathogens:




* Gram-positive

* Aerobic: <u>S. aureus</u> (common), <u>S. pyogenes</u>

* Anaerobic: Propionibacterium, <u>Peptostreptococcus</u>

* Gram-negative

* Aerobic: <u>P. aeruginosa</u> (common)

* Anaerobic (including <u>facultative anaerobes</u>): <u>Bacteroides</u>, <u>E. coli</u>, <u>P. mirabilis</u>, <u>K. pneumoniae</u>

* Fungal: <u>Aspergillus</u>





> [!TIP]
> When a single <u>pathogen</u> is isolated, <u>S. aureus</u> and <u>P. aeruginosa</u> are the most common species isolated. [[3]](/library/scWtd40)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)[[5]](/library/sUWtek0)




* Prior <u>tympanostomy tube placement</u>, especially if:

* ≥ 3 episodes of <u>acute otitis media</u> (<u>AOM</u>) in the preceding 12 months

* Exposure to other children (e.g., in daycare, older siblings)

* <u>Recurrent AOM</u>; see also “<u>Risk factors for AOM</u>.”

* Frequent <u>upper respiratory tract infections</u>  [[5]](/library/sUWtek0)

* Socioeconomic factors

---

## Clinical features

* Painless, recurrent <u>otorrhea</u> for at least ≥ 2 weeks  [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)

* <u>Nonintact tympanic membrane</u> (i.e., a perforation or <u>tympanostomy</u> tube is present)  [[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)

* Additional features may include: [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)

* <u>Hearing loss</u> (in up to 50% of patients)  [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[6]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Acquired <u>cholesteatoma</u>  [[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)[[6]](/library/kIYm1q)

* <u>Mucosal</u> changes of <u>the ear</u> canal  [[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)

* <u>Otomycosis</u> (if fungal etiology)





> [!TIP]
> Patients with CSOM are usually clinically well; signs of systemic illness (e.g., <u>fever</u>) should raise concerns for complications. [[7]](/library/SUWyck0)[[8]](/library/-UWDfk0)[[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)




### Red flags for complications of CSOM [[7]](/library/SUWyck0)[[8]](/library/-UWDfk0)[[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)




* <u>Otalgia</u>

* Signs of systemic illness, e.g., <u>fever</u>

* <u>Focal neurologic signs</u>

* <u>Altered mental status</u>

* <u>Headache</u>

* <u>Clinical features of mastoiditis</u>

* <u>Immunocompromised state</u>  [[10]](/library/12W2gk0)

## Diagnosis

### General principles [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[3]](/library/scWtd40)




* CSOM is a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>;  based on characteristic symptoms and <u>otoscopy</u> confirming perforation of the TM.

* An <u>audiogram</u> should be performed to evaluate for <u>hearing loss</u> and to monitor <u>hearing</u> in response to treatment. [[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)

* Further studies are usually only required for persistent symptoms or suspected complications.





### Further studies [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[3]](/library/scWtd40)[[7]](/library/SUWyck0)




* Bacterial, and possibly fungal, cultures of <u>middle ear</u> <u>aspirate</u>  [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)[[12]](/library/c2Wagk0)

* <u>Neuroimaging</u>

* Symptoms determine the imaging modality and location.

* For potential findings, see “<u>Diagnostics of mastoiditis</u>” and “<u>Otogenic abscess</u>.” [[7]](/library/SUWyck0)[[13]](/library/QkbunF)[[14]](/library/Qmbu28)

* <u>Biopsy</u> of persistent <u>granulation tissue</u> to exclude <u>neoplasia</u> or granulomatous disorders. [[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)

---

## Treatment

### Approach [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)[[6]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Evaluate for <u>red flags for complications of CSOM</u> and if present:

* Urgently consult otolaryngology.

* Obtain relevant diagnostic studies (e.g., <u>neuroimaging</u>, cultures).

* Initiate urgent <u>antimicrobial therapy</u> in consultation with infectious disease (ID).

* For all other patients, determine subtype of CSOM. [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[6]](/library/kIYm1q)[[12]](/library/c2Wagk0)

* <u>Tubotympanic CSOM</u> or <u>posttympanostomy tube CSOM</u>: Initiate <u>conservative management for CSOM</u>.

* <u>Atticoantral CSOM</u>, recurrent CSOM, or persistent symptoms  [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)

* Refer to otolaryngology.

* <u>Surgical management for CSOM</u> may be required.

* All patients: Initiate <u>ongoing management of CSOM</u>.





> [!TIP]
> The goals of treatment are to eradicate the infection and ensure healing of the TM (either spontaneously or through surgical repair). [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)




### Conservative management for CSOM [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)[[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)




* Indications

* <u>Tubotympanic CSOM</u>

* <u>Posttympanostomy tube CSOM</u>

* Preferred: usually determined in consultation with otolaryngology

* Topical <u>antibiotic</u> (usually a <u>fluoroquinolone</u>) with/without a <u>topical steroid</u>, e.g.:   [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)[[16]](/library/IZWY1P0); 

* <u>Ofloxacin</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Ciprofloxacin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE  [[17]](/library/XTW96k0)[[18]](/library/eTWxpk0)

* <u>Ciprofloxacin</u>/<u>dexamethasone</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[19]](/library/YTWn6k0)[[20]](/library/bTWH6k0)

* <u>Aural toilet</u> (unclear benefit)  [[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)[[21]](/library/g2WFSk0)

* Suspected fungal infection: Add a topical <u>antifungal</u> in consultation with ID. [[22]](/library/EfW8Lk0)

* Alternative

* Oral <u>antibiotics</u>  [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)

* Topical <u>antiseptics</u>  [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[9]](/library/TUW6ck0)





> [!WARNING]
> Topical <u>aminoglycoside</u> drops, which are <u>ototoxic</u> to the <u>middle ear</u>, are contraindicated when the <u>tympanic membrane</u> is perforated. [[23]](/library/gR1Fmg0)[[24]](/library/T2W6Sk0)[[25]](/library/32WShk0)




### Surgical management for CSOM [[2]](/library/nz17tj0)[[4]](/library/L_1wKj0)




* Indications

* <u>Atticoantral CSOM</u>

* Recurrent or persistent CSOM

* Any associated <u>urgent complications of CSOM</u>

* Procedures

* <u>Tympanoplasty</u> with or without <u>mastoidectomy</u>

* In individuals with complications, additional surgeries may be indicated.  [[8]](/library/-UWDfk0)[[26]](/library/8UWOUk0)





### Ongoing management of CSOM [[26]](/library/8UWOUk0)[[27]](/library/FUWgUk0)




* Recommend <u>dry ear precautions</u> until the TM has healed. [[26]](/library/8UWOUk0)[[27]](/library/FUWgUk0)

* Advise patients to seek prompt <u>treatment for AOM</u> if symptoms develop.

* For patients with recurrent CSOM [[26]](/library/8UWOUk0)

* Prophylactic <u>antibiotics</u> are not recommended because of the risk of <u>antibiotic</u> resistance.

* Obtain CT of the mastoid to evaluate for potential causes of recurrent disease (e.g., <u>cholesteatoma</u>, mastoid <u>abscess</u> formation).

* Consider surgical management (e.g., <u>tympanoplasty</u>).  [[26]](/library/8UWOUk0)
